title: I Have A Cold
subtitle: Reflections on contagion of viruses and ideas that are sickening.
body_html:
Oh my gosh. It's been a while. My old friend, my nemesis. Cough. Cough. My older sister Alison referred to my robust coughing by screaming, with malicious glee, "Feeding time at the zoo!"  This is because I sounded like a seal or barking like a sea lion. I have a cold again today. Alison never let me live it down.

Welcome to The Frontier Psychiatrists, a daily enough health-themed newsletter.

Subscribe now

COVID changed my relationship to colds. I've had a chronic cough on and off for years. I've written articles about it. At the beginning of residency training, it was so bad that I had post-tussive emesis—that is, coughing so hard you throw up.

That went on for nine months. I got a cardiothoracic CT scan to evaluate what turned out to be a postnasal drip. Before the pandemic, a cough was Embarrassing and annoying, especially when it was non-infectious. But for a long time, we kind of casually infected each other with upper respiratory viruses, which had some relationship with our biology that made sense. I remember looking at pictures of people in East Asia wearing face masks after SARS or MIRS and thinking, a little overreactionary?

Except it wasn't.   That was me being judgmental in the way someone who hasn't been forced to live through a respiratory virus pandemic can casually be.   I look back at that attitude now, and I judge myself harshly. I made a whole podcast series about how strange the pandemic was, from the heart of the storm in New York City. For example, Episode 1, Episode 2, Episode 3, Episode 4, Episode 5, and more. The podcast feed—it’s hot.

I have a cold. I'm not going to the school gala, to the office, or to the gym. I'm going to do everything by Zoom. I'm not going to get anybody else sick. I feel stuffy. My throat is scratchy. All of this used to be kind of par for the course, but now, even though I've tested negative for COVID-19 twice and am appropriately vaccinated, there is a sense of menace.   

I have a cold.   I've had to blow my nose several times already this morning. Then I washed my hands.  Did I do it enough?

There are questions on the Yale-Brown obsessive-compulsive scale about spreading contaminants.   People with OCD will worry that they inadvertently but aggressively spread contaminants.  These fears are beyond what is reasonable.    That is by definition. That is the nature of obsessive-compulsive disorder.  However, the root of those fears?  That's my reality now.  Or an echo of my reality. We should worry that we got other people sick. It shouldn't be an incapacitating worry.

I would go further today. I would argue that there are mimetic illnesses.  Their ideas spread unwellness.   These ideas can be as infectious as an upper respiratory infection and even more deadly.  You could imagine that casual comments putting down women, denying the reality of systematic racism, or mocking people for how they suffer…are all in good fun.  Just locker room talk! Sick ideas can lead to harm and actual sickness.  Some ideas have stood as bulwarks against human deprivation for millennia.   Accountability.   Compassion. Grace. More and more. We have data that depression, without a biologically separate vector like a virus, can be a catching thing.1 We have known for decades that there are contagion effects of death by suicide.2 I remember conversations with the remarkable Mark Gould, M.D., in the heady days of 2020 on the Clubhouse app. His work on contagion remains important.3

We recognize bacteria and viruses as modern miasma—mostly. We under-recognize that ideas can lead to death and dismay, and only after events like the Rwandan Genocide do we see clearly what we could have recognized in advance.4

The thread I am arguing for today? The contagion of bad things, not only biological vectors, should be avoided. If we are in a catching state, with thoughts filled with bile and venom for ourselves or others? Let us be careful.

Share

1

Paz, L. V., Viola, T. W., Milanesi, B. B., Sulzbach, J. H., Mestriner, R. G., Wieck, A., & Xavier, L. L. (2022). Contagious depression: Automatic mimicry and the mirror neuron system - A review. Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews, 134, 104509. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neubiorev.2021.12.032

2

Cheng, Q., Li, H., Silenzio, V., & Caine, E. D. (2014). Suicide contagion: A systematic review of definitions and research utility. PloS one, 9(9), e108724.

3

Lake, A. M., & Gould, M. S. (2014). Suicide clusters and suicide contagion. A concise guide to understanding suicide: Epidemiology, pathophysiology and prevention, 52-61.

4

McDoom, O. S. (2012). Predicting Violence within Genocide: Meso-Level Evidence from Rwanda. Available at SSRN 2206778.
